title: Gregory of Nazianzus
hookLine: a shy poet-bishop who preached on the Trinity in a tiny church and resigned rather than fight

cards: Two students in Athens who know only two roads: one to church, one to their teachers. That's how Gregory remembers himself and Basil, in his speech in Basil's memory.
Gregory, from a small town called Nazianzus, is today's word. He loved books, quiet and poetry. What he didn't love was being in charge.
When his own father, a bishop, made him a priest, Gregory ran away to think it over, and later wrote a long defense of why he'd fled.
And yet this reluctant man was about to be sent into the middle of a fierce religious argument in the empire's new capital.

teach.b: The capital was Constantinople, and the argument was the one we met at Nicaea, still raging. There, the people holding to the Nicene creed were few, and had lost their churches.
So Gregory preached in a small house chapel, given by a relative, and named it Anastasia: resurrection. A small room, standing for a faith he hoped would rise again.
There he preached a series of sermons on God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

teach.h: SERMONS ON GOD, CAREFUL AND HUMBLE.
teach.b: They're careful and humble. He keeps saying that talking about God is dangerous, that God is beyond our words, and that the way to know God is a clean, prayerful life, not winning debates.
Later tradition gave him a title: Gregory the Theologian. Then the tide turned.
A new emperor favored the Nicene side, the great churches were handed back, and Gregory, the shy poet, was put in charge of the city's church.
At the council held there, he presided for a time. And then the fights began, about him. Rival bishops said his appointment broke the rules.

teach.h: CAST ME FORTH INTO THE SEA.
teach.b: By his own account, Gregory reached for the prophet Jonah, who told the sailors in the storm: "Take me up, and cast me forth into the sea; so shall the sea be calm unto you." He resigned.
He went home to Cappadocia, wrote poems, including a long one about his own life, and cared for a small flock. He didn't keep the job. He chose the calm over the chair.

how: Orthodox Christians honor Gregory as a teacher of the faith, calling him the Theologian, and Catholic and other churches keep his feast; his sermons on God are still read.

games.q: you're Gregory, presiding at the council. rivals say your appointment broke the rules, and factions are forming. what do you do?
o: fight it out, you're in the right.
resign, and let the storm calm.
quietly take the side with the most votes.
games.why: he stepped down, reaching for Jonah: take me up, and cast me forth into the sea.

practice: Think of a fight you're in, or about to be in, that doesn't really need to happen, where being right has started to matter more than anything you're defending, and picture it as a boat in a storm.
Ask what would actually be lost if you stepped back: sometimes something real, and then you stay; sometimes only your position. If you pray, bring that fight to God and leave it there for now.

wordCard.voice: Gregory. Basil's friend from Nazianzus, a poet and preacher on the Trinity, who led the church in Constantinople and stepped down rather than keep a fight going.
